solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Extensive view of old queen in a hat

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside it

parts.note: a panama is a lightweight straw hat
O is the standard abbreviation for old
R, for Regina, is the Latin abbreviation for queen

explanation.surface: Someone describes a sweeping view featuring an elderly queen wearing a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a hat' is the container, not 'a' plus something: PANAMA opens after its third letter to take O and R, giving PAN-OR-AMA.
explanation.definitionFit: A panorama is a wide, unbroken outlook over a whole landscape, which is exactly a broad sweeping scene.

clue.text: Man better after hospital admission

indicators.note: admission is letting something in, so one word takes in the other

parts.note: to cap something is to better or outdo it
H is the map-sign abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A patient is feeling better once he has been admitted to hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'better' reads as an adjective about the man's health but is the verb 'to cap', as in capping a story; it swallows H.
explanation.definitionFit: Chap is an informal British word for a fellow or bloke, an ordinary male person.

clue.text: Blunder by scientist ultimately creating panic

indicators.note: ultimately means at the very end, so only a final letter is wanted

parts.note: last letter of the word
a blunder is an error

explanation.surface: A scientist's mistake ends up causing widespread alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists the blunder first, but 'by' lets the scientist's last letter stand in front of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Terror is overwhelming fear, the same state of alarm as panic, so the two nouns are near synonyms.

clue.text: One letting off steam in kitchen?

definitions.text: One letting off steam in kitchen?

parts.words: One letting off steam in kitchen?
parts.note: surface reading: a stressed cook venting frustration at the stove; setter's reading: an appliance that literally puffs out steam when water boils

explanation.walkthrough: 'Letting off steam' is an idiom for releasing anger; here it is taken literally, pointing to an object rather than a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A kettle boils water and releases vapour from its spout, a common appliance found beside every British cooker.

clue.text: Unusual cottage, I think

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal form, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone muses aloud that a particular house is rather odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I think' reads as a hedge, but 'I' belongs to the fodder and 'think' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To cogitate is a formal word for pondering or reflecting at length, so it is a synonym for the verb.

clue.text: Achievement of one's supporters, you might say

indicators.note: what you might say is spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: your feet are what hold you up

explanation.surface: A team's fans are credited with a great accomplishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supporters' suggests fans, but it means the body parts a person stands on.
explanation.definitionFit: A feat is a notable deed accomplished through skill or courage, a direct synonym for a remarkable success.

clue.text: Search me after messing up fine material

indicators.note: messing up something disorders it, so the letters come out jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs 'search me' after ruining an expensive piece of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Search me' is the idiom for 'I don't know', but here both words are fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is a soft luxurious wool from Kashmir goats, a classic example of costly textile.

clue.text: Old vicar coming back no more

parts.note: O abbreviates old

indicators.note: coming back is travelling the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Rev is short for Reverend, a vicar's title

explanation.surface: A retired clergyman returns to the parish now that he has stopped working.
explanation.walkthrough: Rev, short for Reverend, is the title a vicar carries; turned round it follows O.
explanation.definitionFit: When something is finished it is said to be done with, ended and gone, which is what 'no more' also means.

clue.text: Policeman in helicopter losing height

indicators.note: losing something means it goes missing, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: chopper is slang for a helicopter
H is the abbreviation for height

explanation.surface: A police officer in a helicopter drops altitude.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the H from CHOPPER to leave the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Copper is informal British slang for a police officer, the everyday word for a constable.

clue.text: Dance for Oliver, perhaps

definitions.meaning: second meaning: surname of the orphan in the Dickens novel

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a dance routine to perform for a boy named Oliver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' shows Oliver is an example: Oliver is one well-known bearer of this surname, from Dickens's 'Oliver Twist'.
explanation.definitionFit: The twist was a hip-swivelling craze popularised by Chubby Checker, and the Dickens orphan carries this surname.

clue.text: Cry after striking husband's hooter

indicators.note: striking something out crosses it off, so a letter is removed

parts.note: a howl is a loud cry
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Someone yelps after hitting her husband on the nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' looks like a blow and 'hooter' like slang for a nose; in fact the H is struck out, and the hooter is a bird that hoots. The ’s stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Owls make a hooting call at night, so a whimsical description of the bird is something that hoots.

clue.text: Spots Her Majesty making a bit of bacon

parts.note: a rash is an outbreak of spots
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher

explanation.surface: The Queen is seen cooking herself a slice of breakfast meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spots' reads as a verb, sees, but is the noun for a skin outbreak.
explanation.definitionFit: A rasher is a single thin slice of bacon or ham, cut for frying at breakfast.

clue.text: Hotel in Donegal rebuilt hastily

parts.note: Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: rebuilding puts the parts together again in a new form

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hotel in the Irish county of Donegal was reconstructed in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' reads as a location but only joins H to the rearranged county name.
explanation.definitionFit: Rushing headlong means going forward with reckless speed, without pausing to think, so it matches the adverb.

clue.text: Candidate in the end failing to pass

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

parts.note: final letter of the word
a lapse is a failing or slip

explanation.surface: An examinee ends up not getting through the test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'failing to pass' reads as one phrase about an exam; it splits into the noun 'failing' and the definition 'to pass'.
explanation.definitionFit: Time is said to elapse when it goes by, so the verb means moving on in the sense of hours passing.

clue.text: Strange European initially somehow becoming an army officer

indicators.note: somehow suggests an unknown method, so the letters are arranged in some other way

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: An odd foreigner mysteriously finds himself promoted to a military rank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' looks like the anagram signal, but it is the fodder; the last adverb before 'becoming' does the rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant is a senior non-commissioned rank in the army, loosely called an officer in everyday speech.

clue.text: Charlie unfortunately keeping one in French port

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so one word holds another

parts.note: alas is an exclamation of regret
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Poor Charlie is stuck in a harbour town across the Channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' reads as a comment on Charlie's luck but is the word ALAS, which then holds I.
explanation.definitionFit: Calais is the ferry harbour on the northern coast of France nearest to Dover.

clue.text: Trial of MP involved in deal

indicators.note: being involved in something puts you inside it

parts.note: a sale is a deal or transaction
taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician goes on trial over a shady business arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trial' suggests a court case, but it means a try-out portion.
explanation.definitionFit: A sample is a small portion given out to test or try something, as with a free trial.

clue.text: Tired Shakespearean king stuck in past

indicators.note: something stuck in something else is lodged inside it

parts.note: to go by is to go past
King Lear is Shakespeare's tragic monarch

explanation.surface: An exhausted old monarch from the plays cannot move on from his history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'past' reads as a noun, history, but it is the preposition BY, as in 'walk by'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bleary eyes are dim and blurred from lack of sleep, so the adjective describes a weary, worn-out state.

clue.text: Execute British boss in possession of ecstasy

indicators.note: to be in possession of something is to hold it, so letters are held inside

parts.note: B abbreviates British
the head is the boss
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A British manager caught carrying illegal drugs faces the ultimate punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: B and HEAD together hold E, which slips in between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Beheading is killing by cutting off the head, one specific method of putting a condemned person to death.

clue.text: Terrific, parrot having heart transplant?

indicators.note: a transplant swaps an organ for a new one, so the central letter is replaced

parts.note: to parrot is to copy, which is to ape

explanation.surface: Someone is delighted that a pet parrot has come through major heart surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parrot' is the verb, to mimic. Its middle letter P is swapped for a C; the new heart is not clued, which the question mark acknowledges.
explanation.definitionFit: Ace is informal praise meaning excellent or first-rate, so it works as an adjective for something wonderful.

clue.text: Faith on island weak for the most part

indicators.note: the most part of something is all but a little, so the last letter goes

parts.note: IS is the abbreviation for island
a lame excuse is a weak one

explanation.surface: Belief among an island community is fading for the most part.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' simply places one piece after the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Islam is the monotheistic religion of Muslims, one example of a religious belief system.

clue.text: Said superstar is out of work

indicators.note: said means spoken out loud, so only the sound counts

parts.note: a superstar is an idol

explanation.surface: A famous celebrity is reported to be unemployed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Said' looks like 'the aforementioned', but it signals the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle can describe people without jobs or machines standing unused, so jobless is one of its senses.

clue.text: Terrible mistake made by a monkey

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the loud-voiced South American primate

explanation.surface: A dreadful error has been committed by a monkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'made by' makes the monkey sound like the culprit; it only links two meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: A glaring embarrassing blunder is called this informally, and the howler monkey of Central America shares the name.

clue.text: Drink Strongbow in extra-large bottles

indicators.note: to bottle is to enclose, so the phrase holds the letters inside it

parts.note: straddles the first three words of the phrase

explanation.surface: A popular brand of cider is sold in jumbo bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: Strongbow is a British brand of cider, which pulls the mind towards cider; the letters run across 'Strongbow in extra'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wine is fermented grape juice, an alcoholic beverage, so it is a straightforward example of a drink.

clue.text: Style of beer knocked back at noon

indicators.note: knocked back means turned backwards, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: A particular type of beer is downed at midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked back' suggests drinking the beer; in the wordplay it sends ALE backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Élan is flair and energetic confidence, the dash of panache that makes up personal style.

clue.text: Left deserving a little of what to Pope is dangerous

definitions.text: a little of what to Pope is dangerous

parts.note: L abbreviates left
to earn praise is to deserve it

explanation.surface: A wry nod to a famous line of poetry about the dangers of partial knowledge.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Pope, the 18th-century English poet, wrote 'A little learning is a dang'rous thing', which the definition quotes around.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation completes itself: in Pope's Essay on Criticism a small amount of knowledge is called hazardous.
